questions.title: Composition of Nissl bodies
questions.question: Nissl bodies consist of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Synaptic vesicles are small membrane-bound sacs of neurotransmitter clustered at the axon terminal (presynaptic bouton), not the basophilic cytoplasmic masses of the perikaryon that are stained as Nissl bodies.
explanations.B: Correct. Nissl bodies (Nissl substance) are the basophilic granular masses of the neuronal cell body and dendrites, composed of rough endoplasmic reticulum studded with ribosomes together with free polyribosomes. Their abundant ribosomal RNA is what gives them their strong basophilia and reflects the neuron's high rate of protein synthesis. They extend into the dendrites but are absent from the axon hillock and axon, a classic identifying feature, and their dispersal (chromatolysis) after axonal injury mirrors this protein-synthesising role.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The Golgi apparatus is a separate organelle that packages and modifies proteins; it is argyrophilic (silver-staining) rather than basophilic and is not what the term Nissl body denotes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lysosomes and lipofuscin (an age-related residual-body pigment) are distinct cytoplasmic components; lipofuscin does accumulate with age in neurons but is not the basophilic Nissl substance.

questions.learning_objective: State that Nissl bodies are composed of rough endoplasmic reticulum and ribosomes (including free polyribosomes), accounting for their cytoplasmic basophilia.

questions.title: Location of bipolar neurons
questions.question: Bipolar neurons are present in:

options.D: Mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve

explanations.A: Correct. Bipolar neurons carry two processes — a single dendrite and a single axon — extending from opposite poles of the cell body, and in the adult they occur in the special sensory pathways: the retina, the olfactory epithelium, and the vestibular (Scarpa's) and cochlear (spiral) ganglia of the vestibulocochlear nerve. The vestibular ganglion is therefore the correct location among the options offered. This bipolar morphology suits their role as a first-order relay in a sensory pathway.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The neurons of the spinal (dorsal root) ganglia are pseudounipolar — a single process leaves the cell body and divides into central and peripheral branches — not bipolar.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sympathetic (autonomic) ganglion cells are multipolar neurons with many dendrites, not bipolar.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve contains pseudounipolar primary sensory neurons (a unique CNS location for such cells), not bipolar neurons.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the vestibular (and cochlear) ganglia as sites of bipolar neurons, distinguishing them from the pseudounipolar spinal ganglia and mesencephalic nucleus and the multipolar sympathetic ganglia.

questions.title: Unencapsulated sensory nerve ending
questions.question: One of the following is classified as unencapsulated:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The Golgi tendon organ is an encapsulated proprioceptor enclosed in a connective-tissue capsule at the myotendinous junction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Meissner's (tactile) corpuscles are encapsulated mechanoreceptors of the dermal papillae, wrapped in a thin connective-tissue capsule.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Krause end bulbs are encapsulated receptors, a coiled nerve terminal surrounded by a thin connective-tissue capsule.
explanations.D: Correct. Sensory nerve endings are classified as encapsulated (enclosed in a connective-tissue capsule — Meissner, Pacinian, Ruffini and Krause corpuscles and the Golgi tendon organ) or unencapsulated (naked terminals lacking such a capsule). Free nerve endings are the prototypical unencapsulated ending: bare terminal branches, mostly of pain and temperature fibres, ramifying among epithelial and connective-tissue cells without any capsule. Merkel discs and peritrichial (hair-follicle) endings are the other unencapsulated types.

questions.learning_objective: Classify free nerve endings as unencapsulated sensory receptors, distinguishing them from the encapsulated Golgi tendon organ, Meissner's corpuscle and Krause end bulb.

questions.title: Cell forming CNS myelin
questions.question: Cell type that forms the myelin sheath around myelinated axons in the CNS:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ependymal cells line the ventricles and central canal; they do not form myelin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Schwann cells myelinate axons in the PERIPHERAL nervous system, each internode formed by one Schwann cell; they are not the myelinating cell of the CNS.
explanations.C: Correct. Oligodendrocytes are the myelinating neuroglia of the central nervous system: a single oligodendrocyte extends several processes, each wrapping an internode of myelin around a different CNS axon (unlike a Schwann cell, which myelinates only one internode of one peripheral axon). This one-cell-to-many-axons arrangement is a defining CNS feature, and oligodendrocyte loss underlies central demyelinating disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Astrocytes provide structural and metabolic support and contribute to the blood-brain barrier; they do not form myelin.

questions.learning_objective: State that oligodendrocytes form CNS myelin (one cell myelinating several axons), distinguishing them from peripheral Schwann cells.

questions.title: Why white matter appears white
questions.question: White matter appears white because of the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. White matter is well vascularised; blood vessels do not account for its colour, and their presence would if anything add colour rather than whiteness.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The central nervous system contains essentially no collagen/connective tissue within its substance; there are no abundant collagen fibres to colour white matter.
explanations.C: Incorrect. White matter is rich in glial cells (oligodendrocytes and astrocytes); their presence, not absence, is normal there.
explanations.D: Correct. White matter owes its pale, glistening appearance to its dense population of MYELINATED axons: the lipid-rich myelin sheaths scatter light and give the tissue its white colour, which is why fibre tracts look white while neuron-cell-body-rich grey matter looks grey. This colour difference is the gross correlate of the histological distinction between myelinated tracts and cell-body-dense cortex/nuclei.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that white matter appears white because of its abundant myelinated axons (lipid-rich myelin), distinguishing it from grey matter.

questions.title: Neuroglia responsible for CSF movement
questions.question: Which type of neuroglia is responsible for movement of cerebrospinal fluid?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Microglia are the small phagocytic (immune) cells of the CNS; they have no role in propelling cerebrospinal fluid.
explanations.B: Correct. Ependymal cells form the ciliated simple epithelium lining the ventricles, cerebral aqueduct and central canal; the coordinated beating of their apical cilia helps propel and circulate the cerebrospinal fluid through the ventricular system. Their location at the CSF-tissue interface and their motile cilia are exactly what suit them to moving CSF, distinguishing them from the other neuroglia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Astrocytes provide structural/metabolic support and contribute to the blood-brain barrier; they are not ciliated and do not move CSF.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Oligodendrocytes form CNS myelin; they play no part in CSF circulation.

questions.learning_objective: Identify ependymal cells (ciliated ventricular lining) as the neuroglia that help move cerebrospinal fluid.

questions.title: Connective-tissue sensory receptor
questions.question: One of the following is a connective tissue receptor:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Peritrichial (hair-follicle) endings wrap around hair follicles and are classified as epithelial (unencapsulated) receptors, not connective-tissue receptors.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The muscle spindle is a receptor located within skeletal muscle (a proprioceptor among the intrafusal muscle fibres), classified as a muscular receptor rather than a connective-tissue receptor.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The organ of Corti is the specialised receptor of hearing in the cochlea, a special-sense receptor, not a general connective-tissue receptor.
explanations.D: Correct. Sensory receptors are grouped by their location into epithelial, connective-tissue and special-sense receptors; the connective-tissue receptors are the encapsulated endings lying in dermis/connective tissue — Meissner's and Pacinian corpuscles, Ruffini endings, Krause end bulbs and the Golgi tendon organ. Krause's end bulb, an encapsulated ending in the connective tissue of the dermis and mucous membranes, is therefore the connective-tissue receptor among the options.

questions.learning_objective: Classify Krause's end bulb as an encapsulated connective-tissue receptor, distinguishing it from epithelial (peritrichial), muscular (muscle spindle) and special-sense (organ of Corti) receptors.

questions.title: Why the CNS is soft in consistency
questions.question: The central nervous system is soft because:

options.A: It consists of neurons joined by connective tissue
options.B: It is rich in blood vessels
options.C: It does not contain connective tissue

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neurons in the CNS are not held together by connective tissue; support is provided by neuroglia, so this description is wrong.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Although the CNS is vascular, its blood supply is not what determines its soft consistency.
explanations.C: Correct. The substance of the central nervous system contains essentially no connective tissue internally (collagen/fibrous stroma is confined to the meninges and the perivascular spaces); mechanical support instead comes from the neuroglial framework. Because it lacks the tough fibrous connective-tissue stroma that firms up most organs, the CNS is soft and gel-like in consistency. This absence of internal connective tissue is a defining histological feature of nervous tissue.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The CNS does not contain fat (adipose) cells in its substance; myelin lipid is intracellular in glial membranes, not stored in fat cells.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that the CNS is soft because its substance lacks connective tissue, being supported instead by neuroglia.

questions.title: Epithelium lining the central canal
questions.question: The central canal of the spinal cord is lined by which epithelium?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The central canal is not lined by simple squamous epithelium; that lining (mesothelium/endothelium) belongs to serous cavities and vessels.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Stratified squamous epithelium is a protective surface epithelium (e.g. epidermis, oesophagus), not the lining of the central canal.
explanations.C: Correct. The central canal, like the ventricular system, is lined by ependyma — a simple cuboidal to low-columnar epithelium whose cells bear apical cilia (and microvilli). The cilia help move cerebrospinal fluid, and this ciliated simple cuboidal/columnar ependymal lining is the correct description among the options. Its single layer at the CSF interface is what makes it simple (not stratified) and ciliated.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The ependyma is ciliated, so a 'non-ciliated' columnar description is wrong; the presence of cilia is a defining feature of the central-canal lining.

questions.learning_objective: State that the central canal is lined by ciliated simple cuboidal (ependymal) epithelium.

questions.title: Histological composition of the pia mater
questions.question: The pia mater is formed of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The meninges are not true epithelia; the pia is not a simple squamous epithelium (that lining belongs to serous cavities and vessels).
explanations.B: Incorrect. The pia is not a simple columnar epithelium; columnar epithelia line surfaces such as the gut, not the meninges.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ciliated simple columnar epithelium lines the respiratory tract and (as ependyma) the ventricles/central canal, not the pia mater.
explanations.D: Correct. The pia mater, like the other leptomeninges, is a delicate connective-tissue membrane composed of flattened, modified fibroblasts (leptomeningeal/meningothelial cells) together with fine collagen and elastic fibres and the pial vessels — it is mesenchymal in origin, not an epithelium. This is why the pia is classified histologically as modified fibroblasts rather than any surface epithelium, and it closely invests the brain and spinal-cord surface, dipping into the sulci.

questions.learning_objective: State that the pia mater is composed of modified (flattened) fibroblasts, a connective-tissue membrane rather than an epithelium.

questions.title: Target of cerebellar climbing fibres
questions.question: One of the following is true about a climbing fibre of the cerebellum:

options.A: It arises from the pontine nuclei

explanations.A: Incorrect. Climbing fibres arise from the inferior olivary nucleus of the medulla; it is the MOSSY fibres that arise from the pontine nuclei (and spinal cord/vestibular nuclei).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Synapsing with granule cells (in the glomeruli of the granular layer) is the property of MOSSY fibres, not climbing fibres.
explanations.C: Correct. Each climbing fibre arises from the contralateral inferior olivary nucleus and ascends to wind around ('climb') the dendritic tree of a single Purkinje cell, forming a powerful one-to-one excitatory synapse — a single climbing-fibre volley evokes a complex spike in that Purkinje cell. This direct climbing-fibre-to-Purkinje-cell relationship is the defining feature that distinguishes climbing fibres from mossy fibres (which act on Purkinje cells only indirectly, via granule-cell parallel fibres).
explanations.D: Incorrect. Climbing fibres are EXCITATORY (glutamatergic); the inhibitory influence on Purkinje cells comes from cortical interneurons (basket, stellate) and the Purkinje cells themselves are the inhibitory output of the cortex.

questions.learning_objective: State that cerebellar climbing fibres (from the inferior olive) form a direct excitatory synapse on Purkinje cells, distinguishing them from granule-cell-targeting mossy fibres.

questions.title: First-order neuron for facial proprioception
questions.question: The first-order neuron in the proprioception pathway from the face and head is located in the:

options.C: Spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve
options.D: Mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve

explanations.A: Incorrect. Most trigeminal primary sensory neurons (for touch, pain and temperature of the face) lie in the trigeminal ganglion, but the primary neurons for PROPRIOCEPTION are the exception — their cell bodies are not in the ganglion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The dorsal root ganglia hold first-order sensory neurons for the body/limbs, not for the face and head.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve is a SECOND-order (relay) nucleus for pain and temperature from the face, not the site of the first-order proprioceptive neuron.
explanations.D: Correct. The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve is unique in the entire nervous system: it contains the cell bodies of the FIRST-order (primary) sensory neurons for proprioception from the muscles of mastication and other facial/head structures — the only primary sensory neurons whose cell bodies lie within the CNS rather than in a peripheral ganglion. This exceptional intra-CNS location of a primary proprioceptive neuron is exactly what the question tests.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve as the site of the first-order proprioceptive neuron for the face (a unique intra-CNS primary sensory neuron).
